messages.author: 0dd5b3b27f5f2402
messages.subject: Supervised Classification
parts:
Hi

I am new to Bayesian modelling and MCMC / Stan so please forgive all rookie mistakes... 

I am trying to construct a minimal working example of a Bayesian classifier for labeled data that should work for my requirements. Let us assume that 1D training samples X = {x_i} from 
every class (label) c_i are generated by some normal distribution with unknown \mu_i and \sigma_i specific to class c_i. So for a new test pattern x_new we know that:

P(c_i | x_new, X) = P(x_new | c_i, X) P(c_i) / (\sum_j (P(x_new | c_j, X) P(c_j))  

where we can further write P(x_new | c_i, X) = \int d \theta P(x_new | c_i, \theta_i) P(\theta_i | c_i, X) where \theta_i = (\mu_i, \sigma_i)

So to get distribution P(\theta_i|c_i, X) is pretty trivial using the following Stan code:

data {
    int<lower=0> N; // num of training set samples 
    int<lower=1> M; // num of classes
    real X[N];  //training data
    int<lower=1, upper=M> C[N]; // class for sample n
   real x_new; //new test pattern to classify

}
transformed data {}
parameters {
    real mu[M]; 
    real sigma[M]; 
    real x_pred[M];
}
transformed parameters {}
model {
    //likelihood
    for (n in 1:N) 
        X[n] ~ normal(mu[C[n]], sigma[C[n]]) 
       
    //predictive posterior
    for (m in 1:M)
       x_pred[m] ~ normal(mu[m], sigma[m]) 
        
}
generated quantities {
}

I probably don't need the predictive posterior, but just used it as a sanity check.
What I do not understand how to do in Stan is the marginalisation (integral/sum) over \theta to get the expected likelihood (and evidence
follows trivially) and then find P(c_i | x_new). What I can do is 

generated quantities{

    real x_new_log_likelihood[M];
    for (m in 1:M)
        x_new_log_likelihood[m] <- normal_log(x_new, mu[m], sigma[m])

}

And then in Python calculated the mean of 'x_new_log_likelihood' for every class (actually doing the required transformations because log \sum is not equal to \sum log) and plug in some priors for P(c_i) and just calculate
P(c_i | x_new) in Python directly. Is there a better way I can do all of this in Stan directly? I hope my explanation is sufficient. I have looked at the 
Naive Bayes example in the manual and I think it should be the same as what I want, but the classification for a new test pattern is not part of the example if I understand
it correctly. 

Regards
Karl

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Supervised Classification
parts:
Stan will do this all for you pretty much automatically.
The manual has some examples of how to do the predictive
distributions within Stan (that is, you use MCMC for
the integral).

As to the normalized category probabilities, you just
need to normalize:

vector[K] lp;
simplex[K] log_theta;

log_theta = lp - log_sum_exp(lp);

This assumes lp[k] = p(y | k) * p(k),
where p(y|k) is probably of observation given category k
and p(k) is the marginal probability of categories.

Then log_theta[k] is log Pr[C = k | y].

exp(theta) = exp(lp) / sum(exp(lp))

- Bob

parts:
That's right other than that it should be -log(M)
rather than 1/M, because everythng's on the log scale.

theta is a vector. And you can do the same thing
for more predictions.

Basically, it's just Bayes's rule coded in Stan.
I thought we had a "naive Bayes" classifier example, but
we don't. I'll add one:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1238#issuecomment-234316954

- Bob

P.S. As of Stan 2.10, the syntax is

normal_lpdf(x_new | ...)

rather than

normal_log(x_new, ...)

[the "lpdf" is for "log probability density function"].

Also, we're now using "=" instead of "<-" for assignment.

We'll still support the old syntax for quite a while.

Pr[C = k | x_new, x, y] is a single value, but then it's a vector
when you consider all k values.

The final output is a sample from the posterior consisting of
a sequence of draws. You can get a single expectation by
averaging, and you can also get uncertainty in that estimate by
looking at quantiles. It's standard posterior predictive inference,
which averages over the posterior.

Pr[C = k | x_new, x, y]

= INTEGRAL_theta Pr[C = k | x_new, theta] p(theta | x, y) d.theta

where theta are your parameters.

- Bob

I wanted to marginalise out theta when calculating Pr[x = x_new | x, theta] and then calculate the class assignment posteriors Pr[C = k | x_new, x] using that result.

On Friday, July 22, 2016 at 7:00:50 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Pr[C = k | x_new, x, y] is a single value, but then it's a vector
when you consider all k values.

The final output is a sample from the posterior consisting of
a sequence of draws.  You can get a single expectation by
averaging, and you can also get uncertainty in that estimate by
looking at quantiles.  It's standard posterior predictive inference,
which averages over the posterior.

  Pr[C = k | x_new, x, y]

  = INTEGRAL_theta Pr[C = k | x_new, theta] p(theta | x, y) d.theta

where theta are your parameters.

- Bob



> On Jul 21, 2016, at 2:06 PM, Karl Möller <ka...@excors.net> wrote:
>
> Ah yes, -log(M) obviously. More predictions I I think understand, what I am not fully understand is why I get a vector if I only predict for a single scalar. Or I think I do, but maybe
> it is not exactly what I want. If I calculate P(C=k | x_new) mathematically, that should be a single value right? As far as I understand, the generated_quantities
> block gets executed on every draw from the posterior p(mu, sigma), so after a specific mu_i, sigma_i is sampled, a value for theta is generated. So after Stan runs,
> I get as many different thetas as there are different mu_i, sigma_i. So if I want my single value, I should take the mean of the thetas in Python after Stan has run?
>
> Am I run or am I missing something? Also thanks for telling me about the new syntax, I have been looking at the PyStan manual which is still 2.9.
>
> Regards
> Karl

> On Thursday, July 21, 2016 at 7:01:45 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> That's right other than that it should be -log(M)
> rather than 1/M, because everythng's on the log scale.
>
> theta is a vector.  And you can do the same thing
> for more predictions.  
>
> Basically, it's just Bayes's rule coded in Stan.
> I thought we had a "naive Bayes" classifier example, but
> we don't.  I'll add one:
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1238#issuecomment-234316954
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  As of Stan 2.10, the syntax is
>
>   normal_lpdf(x_new | ...)
>
> rather than
>
>   normal_log(x_new, ...)
>
> [the "lpdf" is for "log probability density function"].
>
> Also, we're now using "=" instead of "<-" for assignment.
>
> We'll still support the old syntax for quite a while.

> > On Wednesday, July 20, 2016 at 10:04:54 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Stan will do this all for you pretty much automatically.
> > The manual has some examples of how to do the predictive
> > distributions within Stan (that is, you use MCMC for
> > the integral).
> >
> > As to the normalized category probabilities, you just
> > need to normalize:
> >
> >   vector[K] lp;
> >   simplex[K] log_theta;
> >
> >   log_theta = lp - log_sum_exp(lp);
> >
> > This assumes lp[k] = p(y | k) * p(k),
> > where p(y|k) is probably of observation given category k
> > and p(k) is the marginal probability of categories.
> >
> > Then log_theta[k] is log Pr[C = k | y].  
> >
> >   exp(theta) = exp(lp) / sum(exp(lp))
> >
> > - Bob

> > > I am trying to construct a minimal working example of a Bayesian classifier for labeled data that should work for my requirements. Let us assume that 1D training samples X = {x_i} from
> > > every class (label) c_i are generated by some normal distribution with unknown \mu_i and \sigma_i specific to class c_i. So for a new text pattern x_new we know that:
> > >
> > > P(c_i | x_new, X) = P(x_new | c_i, X) P(c_i) / (\sum_j (P(x_new | c_j, X) P(c_j))  
> > >
> > > where we can further write P(x_new | c_i, X) = \int d \theta P(x_new | c_i, \theta_i) P(\theta_i | c_i, X) where \theta_i = (\mu_i, \sigma_i)
> > >
> > > So to get distribution P(\theta_i|c_i, X) is pretty trivial using the following Stan code:
> > >
> > > data {
> > >     int<lower=0> N; // num of training set samples
> > >     int<lower=1> M; // num of classes
> > >     real X[N];  //training data
> > >     int<lower=1, upper=M> C[N]; // class for score n
> > >    real x_new; //new test pattern to classify
> > >
> > > }
> > > transformed data {}
> > > parameters {
> > >     real mu[M];
> > >     real sigma[M];
> > >     real x_pred[M];
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters {}
> > > model {
> > >     //likelihood
> > >     for (n in 1:N)
> > >         scores[n] ~ normal(mu[C[n]], sigma[C[n]])
> > >        
> > >     //predictive posterior
> > >     for (m in 1:M)
> > >        x_pred[m] ~ normal(mu[m], sigma[m])
> > >        
> > > }
> > > generated quantities {
> > > }
> > >
> > > I probably don't need the predictive posterior, but just used it as a sanity check.
> > > What I do not understand how to do in Stan is the marginalisation (integral/sum) over \theta to get the expected likelihood (and evidence
> > > follows trivially) and then find P(c_i | x_new). What I can do is

> > >     real x_new_log_likelihood[M];
> > >     for (m in 1:M)
> > >         new_score_log_likelihood[m] <- normal_log(x_new)
> > >
> > > }
